---
title: "Install Claude Code"
subtitle: "From zero to a working session in about twenty minutes."
---

This page walks you through getting Claude Code on your machine and running
it for the first time. It assumes you have **never** used the terminal in
anger before. If you're a terminal regular, skim past the basics.

## What you need

- A Mac, a Windows machine with WSL, or a Linux box. (Most economists are
  on a Mac; the rest of this page assumes that. The differences for
  Windows/Linux are tiny and noted where they matter.)
- An **Anthropic account** at [claude.ai](https://claude.ai). A free
  account works to start; you'll be prompted to set up billing the first
  time you use Claude Code.
- About 20 minutes.

## Step 1 — Open a terminal

On a Mac:

- Press `Cmd + Space` to open Spotlight.
- Type `Terminal` and hit `Return`.
- A small window with a blinking prompt appears. That's your terminal.

::: {.callout-tip}
The terminal is just another app. The only commands you'll need are the
ones on this page; you don't need to learn the rest.
:::

## Step 2 — Install Node.js (if you don't have it)

Claude Code is distributed as a Node.js package. Check whether you already
have Node:

```bash
node --version
```

If that prints something like `v20.11.0`, you're set — skip to Step 3.

If it says "command not found", install Node from
[nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org). Pick the **LTS** download, run the
installer, accept the defaults. When it's done, close and reopen the
terminal, then re-run `node --version` to confirm.

::: {.callout-note}
**Mac users with Homebrew** can install with `brew install node` instead.
**Windows users** install Node inside WSL, not on Windows directly.
:::

## Step 3 — Install Claude Code

In the terminal, run:

```bash
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
```

This downloads Claude Code and makes the `claude` command available
system-wide. It takes a minute or two. When it's done, verify:

```bash
claude --version
```

::: {.callout-warning}
If you see a permission error mentioning `EACCES` or `permission denied`,
**don't** prefix the command with `sudo`. Instead, follow the
[npm fix-permissions instructions](https://docs.npmjs.com/resolving-eacces-permissions-errors-when-installing-packages-globally).
This is a one-time fix and protects you from a class of problems later.
:::

## Step 4 — Point Claude Code at one of your projects

Pick a project folder you'd like Claude Code to work in. **Do not start
with your most sensitive project.** Pick a paper draft, a teaching repo, or
a side project. In the terminal, change into that folder:

```bash
cd ~/Desktop/some-paper-draft
```

Then run:

```bash
claude
```

The first time you run it, you'll be prompted to log in (a browser tab
will open) and to choose a few preferences. Accept the defaults.

You're now at the Claude Code prompt. It looks like a chat input but
everything you type is being read by an agent that can see — and edit —
the files in this folder.

## Step 5 — Try it on something small

Three good first prompts, in increasing order of "letting it do things":

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Prompt 1 — read-only**

> "What is in this folder? Give me a one-paragraph summary of what this
> project does."

Claude will list files, peek at a few, and summarize. You'll see it call
out tools like `Read` and `Bash`. Nothing is modified.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Prompt 2 — small edit, with review**

> "Add a comment at the top of every `.do` file naming the script and what
> it does. Show me each diff before applying."

Claude proposes a change per file — each diff is the exact lines that
would change — and you approve or reject each one.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Prompt 3 — real work**

> "Read `paper.tex` and tell me which references in the bibliography are
> never cited. Then remove the unused ones."

This reads files, runs analysis, and edits. You approve the deletion.
:::

## Step 6 — Quit and come back

To leave a Claude Code session, type `/exit` or press `Ctrl-C` twice.

To come back later, just `cd` into the same folder and run `claude` again.
If you add a `CLAUDE.md` file to the project (covered
[later](../workflow/memory-and-claude-md.qmd)), Claude reads it at the
start of every session, so it doesn't start from zero.

## Where to go next

- **[Use Claude Code inside VS Code](vscode.qmd)** — recommended if you're
  coming from RStudio, Stata, or Matlab. The diff view, clickable file
  paths, and built-in Git make the agentic loop much easier to follow.
- [Plan mode, todos, slash commands](plan-mode-and-todo.qmd) — the three
  features that make Claude Code feel like a research assistant rather
  than a chatbot.
- [LaTeX paper editing](../examples/latex-paper.qmd) — a fully worked
  example.

::: {.callout-warning}
**Before you point Claude Code at a project with confidential or
restricted-access data**, read [Confidential
data](../pitfalls/confidential-data.qmd). Some data should never go to a
cloud LLM, full stop.
:::
